questionSections.title: The benefits of humour
questionSections.summary:
In one study at Australian National University, randomly chosen groups of participants were shown one of three videos, each designed to generate a different kind of 32 ................. . When all participants were then given a deliberately frustrating task to do, it was found that those who had watched the 33 ................. video persisted with the task for longer and tried harder to accomplish the task than either of the other two groups.

A second study in which participants were asked to perform a particularly 34 ................. task produced similar results. According to researchers David Cheng and Lu Wang, these findings suggest that humour not only reduces 35 ................. and helps build social connections but it may also have a 36 ................. effect on the body and mind.

instructions: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

questionSections.heading: Questions 37–40

questions.prompt: reference to an appealing way of using dance that the writer is not proposing
questions.evidence: That is not to suggest everyone should dance their way to work, however healthy and happy it might make us
synonymSubstitutions: appealing way = healthy and happy
is not proposing = is not to suggest
questions.distractors: F discusses embodied methods, but only B presents the appealing dance-to-work idea and explicitly rejects proposing it.

questions.prompt: an example of a contrast between past and present approaches to building
questions.evidence: Whereas medieval builders improvised and adapted construction ... building designs are now conceived and stored in media technologies
synonymSubstitutions: past approaches = medieval builders improvised and adapted
present approaches = designs are now conceived and stored in media technologies
contrast = Whereas ... now
questions.distractors: D gives a modern planning failure but no past-present comparison; C contains the explicit Whereas-now contrast.

questions.prompt: mention of an objective of both dance and engineering
questions.evidence: Yet it shares with engineering the aim of designing patterns of movement within limitations of space.
synonymSubstitutions: objective = aim
both dance and engineering = choreography shares with engineering
questions.distractors: G recommends learning from choreography, but only F states the shared aim of dance and engineering.

questions.prompt: reference to an unforeseen problem arising from ignoring the climate
questions.evidence: They failed to take into account that purpose-built street cafés could not operate in the hot sun without the protective awnings common in older buildings, and would need energy-consuming air conditioning instead
synonymSubstitutions: unforeseen problem = failed to take into account / unexpected results
ignoring the climate = overlooking the hot sun
questions.distractors: E describes flawed transport models without a climate consequence; D links the overlooked hot sun to unusable cafes and extra air conditioning.

questions.prompt: why some measures intended to help people are being reversed
questions.evidence: These barriers don’t just make it harder to cross the road: they divide communities and decrease opportunities for healthy transport. As a result, many are now being removed
synonymSubstitutions: measures intended to help people = engineering solution to pedestrian safety
being reversed = being removed
why = divide communities and decrease opportunities
questions.distractors: D explains a failed development, not reversal of a safety measure; E states the harms and that guard rails are now being removed.

questions.prompt: reference to how transport has an impact on human lives
questions.evidence: The ways we travel affect our physical and mental health, our social lives, our access to work and culture, and the air we breathe.
synonymSubstitutions: transport = the ways we travel
has an impact on = affect
human lives = health, social lives, access, and air
questions.distractors: E gives narrower effects of guard rails, whereas A explicitly lists broad effects of transport on human lives.

questions.prompt: Guard rails were introduced on British roads to improve the 7 __________ of pedestrians
questions.evidence: an engineering solution to pedestrian safety
synonymSubstitutions: were introduced to improve = were an engineering solution to
the safety of pedestrians = pedestrian safety
questions.distractors: Pedestrians is already supplied and flow belongs to traffic. The noun safety is copied exactly and satisfies ONE WORD ONLY.

questions.prompt: while ensuring that the movement of 8 __________ is not disrupted
questions.evidence: models that prioritise the smooth flow of traffic
synonymSubstitutions: movement = flow
is not disrupted = prioritise the smooth flow
questions.distractors: Pedestrians are redirected and slowed, so their movement is not preserved. Flow would make movement of flow; traffic is the exact noun.

questions.prompt: Pedestrians are led to access points, and encouraged to cross one 9 __________ at a time.
questions.evidence: divide the crossing into two – one for each carriageway
synonymSubstitutions: are led to access points = guide pedestrians to specific crossing points
cross one ... at a time = one for each carriageway
questions.distractors: Crossing is tempting, but the crossing is divided into two; pedestrians cross one carriageway at a time, within the one-word limit.

questions.prompt: particularly for less 10 __________ people
questions.evidence: those that are the least mobile
synonymSubstitutions: less = the least
people = those
psychological difficulties = psychological barriers
questions.distractors: Psychological describes barriers, not people. Mobile correctly forms less mobile people and is copied as one word.

questions.prompt: some people cross the road in a 11 __________ way
questions.evidence: encouraging others to make dangerous crossings
synonymSubstitutions: some people = others
cross the road in a ... way = make ... crossings
questions.distractors: Counter-intuitive describes designs, not how people cross. Dangerous transfers exactly from dangerous crossings and fits the one-word limit.

questions.prompt: The guard rails separate 12 __________
questions.evidence: they divide communities
synonymSubstitutions: guard rails = these barriers / they
separate = divide
questions.distractors: Roads and crossings are nearby locations, but the passage says the barriers divide communities; the plural noun also fits the grammar.

questions.prompt: make it more difficult to introduce forms of transport that are 13 __________
questions.evidence: decrease opportunities for healthy transport
synonymSubstitutions: make it more difficult to introduce = decrease opportunities for
forms of transport that are ... = ... transport
questions.distractors: Safety cannot follow are, and pedestrian misses the stated benefit. Healthy is the exact adjective used with transport and is one word.

questions.prompt: a reference to how further disappearance of multiple species could be avoided
questions.evidence: genetic modifications which could prevent mass extinctions in the future
distractors: A describes recreating one species, not preventing future losses.
B concerns Tasmanian devils rather than multiple future extinctions.
C discusses the limits of exact de-extinction.
D concerns ecosystem restoration.
E concerns mammoths, elephants and emissions.
synonymSubstitutions: further disappearance of multiple species ↔ mass extinctions
could be avoided ↔ could prevent

questions.prompt: explanation of a way of reproducing an extinct animal using the DNA of only that species
questions.evidence: using cloning technology to turn the DNA of extinct animals into a fertilised embryo
distractors: B describes ecological effects, not a reproductive method.
C proposes hybridisation using a living species as a template, so it does not use only the extinct animal’s DNA.
D discusses the purpose of replacement.
E and F discuss adaptation and conservation uses.
synonymSubstitutions: reproducing an extinct animal ↔ turn the DNA of extinct animals into a fertilised embryo
using the DNA of only that species ↔ the DNA of extinct animals

questions.prompt: reference to a habitat which has suffered following the extinction of a species
questions.evidence: Since the disappearance of this key species, ecosystems in the eastern US have suffered
distractors: A outlines the technology.
B focuses on disease in Tasmanian devils.
C focuses on whether exact recreation is possible.
E describes a possible future tundra benefit, not a habitat already harmed.
F discusses preventing extinction.
synonymSubstitutions: a habitat ↔ ecosystems in the eastern US
has suffered following the extinction ↔ Since the disappearance ... ecosystems ... have suffered

questions.prompt: mention of the exact point at which a particular species became extinct
questions.evidence: came to an end on 1 September 1914, when the last living specimen died at Cincinnati Zoo
distractors: B mentions extinction without an exact date or event.
C, D, E and F do not state the precise point when a species became extinct.
synonymSubstitutions: the exact point ↔ on 1 September 1914
became extinct ↔ the last living specimen died

questions.prompt: Professor George Church and his team are trying to identify the 18 __________ which enabled mammoths to live in the tundra.
questions.evidence: pinpointing which genetic traits made it possible for mammoths to survive the icy climate of the tundra
distractors: cold resistance is the research focus, but the grammar after ‘identify the’ and the passage wording require ‘genetic traits’.
The limit is NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS; “genetic traits” is the exact two-word phrase, while any longer phrase exceeds the limit.
synonymSubstitutions: identify ↔ pinpointing
enabled mammoths to live in the tundra ↔ made it possible for mammoths to survive the icy climate of the tundra

questions.prompt: physical adaptations to minimise 19 __________
questions.evidence: all for the purpose of reducing heat loss in the tundra
distractors: cold resistance names the broader research theme; the adaptations specifically minimise heat loss.
The limit is NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS; “heat loss” is the exact two-word phrase required by both grammar and evidence.
synonymSubstitutions: minimise ↔ reducing
physical adaptations ↔ smaller ears, thicker hair, and extra insulating fat

questions.prompt: the mammoth-like features of thicker hair, 20 __________ of a reduced size
questions.evidence: Necessary adaptations would include smaller ears, thicker hair
distractors: hair cannot fit because thicker hair is already stated; fat is answered by the following blank.
The limit allows up to two words, but only “ears” fits before “of a reduced size”; “smaller ears” would duplicate the size meaning and break the sentence.
synonymSubstitutions: of a reduced size ↔ smaller
mammoth-like features ↔ Necessary adaptations

questions.evidence: smaller ears, thicker hair, and extra insulating fat
distractors: The answer must name the substance that can be present in a greater amount; ‘insulating’ alone is an adjective and is incomplete.
The official parentheses make “insulating” optional: both “fat” and “insulating fat” satisfy NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS; “insulating” alone is not accepted.
synonymSubstitutions: more ↔ extra
fat ↔ insulating fat

questions.prompt: help to reduce temperatures and decrease 22 __________
questions.evidence: a useful factor in reducing carbon emissions
distractors: temperatures is already supplied in the summary; permafrost is the source whose melting emissions are mitigated, not the thing decreased.
The official parentheses make “carbon” optional: both “emissions” and “carbon emissions” satisfy NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS; longer wording exceeds the limit.
synonymSubstitutions: decrease ↔ reducing
emissions ↔ carbon emissions

questions.prompt: Reintroducing an extinct species to its original habitat could improve the health of a particular species living there.
questions.evidence: The return of thylacines to Tasmania could help to ensure that devils are never again subjected to risks of this kind.
distractors: A/Ben Novak discusses passenger pigeons and forest habitat, not the health of another resident species.
C/Beth Shapiro discusses conservation priorities and extinction causes.
synonymSubstitutions: Reintroducing ↔ The return of thylacines
its original habitat ↔ Tasmania
improve the health ↔ never again subjected to risks of this kind

questions.prompt: It is important to concentrate on the causes of an animal’s extinction.
questions.evidence: She prefers to focus the debate on how this emerging technology could be used to fully understand why various species went extinct in the first place
distractors: A/Ben Novak focuses on replacing extinct species.
B/Michael Archer explains the ecological effect of losing thylacines.
synonymSubstitutions: concentrate on ↔ focus the debate on
the causes of an animal’s extinction ↔ why various species went extinct in the first place

questions.prompt: A species brought back from extinction could have an important beneficial impact on the vegetation of its habitat.
questions.evidence: re-establish that forest disturbance, thereby creating a habitat necessary for a great many other native species to thrive
distractors: B/Michael Archer discusses controlling Tasmanian devil numbers and disease.
C/Beth Shapiro discusses the limits and conservation uses of de-extinction technology.
synonymSubstitutions: beneficial impact on the vegetation ↔ re-establish that forest disturbance
its habitat ↔ creating a habitat necessary for ... native species to thrive

questions.prompt: Our current efforts at preserving biodiversity are insufficient.
questions.evidence: We know that what we are doing today is not enough
distractors: A/Ben Novak argues for ecological replacement.
B/Michael Archer explains a specific Tasmanian ecological problem.
synonymSubstitutions: Our current efforts ↔ what we are doing today
are insufficient ↔ is not enough

questions.prompt: When referring to laughter in the first paragraph, the writer emphasises
questions.evidence: Like other human emotions and expressions, laughter and humour provide psychological scientists with rich resources for studying human psychology, ranging from the development of language to the neuroscience of social perception.

synonymSubstitutions.question: value to scientific research
synonymSubstitutions.passage: provide psychological scientists with rich resources for studying human psychology

distractors.A: Language is only one end of the stated research range, not the main emphasis.
distractors.B: The paragraph says laughter is universal across cultures, not that its principal function is culture.
distractors.D: The passage says laughter exists in some animals, not that it is universal across animal societies.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about Charley Douglass?

options.A: He understood the importance of enjoying humour in a group setting.
options.B: He believed that TV viewers at home needed to be told when to laugh.
options.C: He wanted his shows to appeal to audiences across the social spectrum.
options.D: He preferred shows where audiences were present in the recording studio.

questions.evidence: These were intended to help people at home feel like they were in a social situation, such as a crowded theatre.

synonymSubstitutions.question: enjoying humour in a group setting
synonymSubstitutions.passage: feel like they were in a social situation, such as a crowded theatre

distractors.B: The track created a social atmosphere; the passage does not say viewers needed instructions about when to laugh.
distractors.C: The mixtures of voices concern types of laughter, not appealing across a social spectrum.
distractors.D: He recorded tracks because he disliked the unpredictable laughter of live audiences, so this reverses the passage.

questions.prompt: What makes the Santa Cruz study particularly significant?

options.A: the various different types of laughter that were studied
options.B: the similar results produced by a wide range of cultures
options.C: the number of different academic disciplines involved
options.D: the many kinds of people whose laughter was recorded

questions.evidence: A team made up of more than 30 psychological scientists, anthropologists, and biologists then played these recordings to listeners from 24 diverse societies, from indigenous tribes in New Guinea to city-dwellers in India and Europe. Participants were asked whether they thought the people laughing were friends or strangers. On average, the results were remarkably consistent: worldwide, people’s guesses were correct approximately 60% of the time.

distractors.A: The study used samples from pairs of students; its significance is not a catalogue of laughter types.
distractors.C: Several disciplines participated, but the highlighted result is consistency across societies.
distractors.D: The laughers were English-speaking students; the cultural diversity belonged to the listeners.

questions.prompt: Which of the following happened in the San Diego study?

options.C: Participants who had not met before became friends.
options.D: Some participants were unable to laugh.

questions.evidence: Laughter was recorded as each student took a turn at being teased by the others, involving the use of mildly insulting nicknames.

synonymSubstitutions.question: exchanged roles
synonymSubstitutions.passage: each student took a turn at being teased by the others

distractors.A: The nicknames were mildly insulting; the passage never says anyone became very upset.
distractors.C: The students belonged to fraternity groups; the passage does not report strangers becoming friends.
distractors.D: All students were recorded laughing; inability to laugh is not reported.

questions.prompt: In the fifth paragraph, what did the results of the San Diego study suggest?

options.A: It is clear whether a dominant laugh is produced by a high- or low-status person.
options.B: Low-status individuals in a position of power will still produce submissive laughs.
options.C: The submissive laughs of low- and high-status individuals are surprisingly similar.
options.D: High-status individuals can always be identified by their way of laughing.

questions.evidence: However, high-status individuals were rated as high-status whether they produced their natural dominant laugh or tried to do a submissive one.

synonymSubstitutions.question: can always be identified
synonymSubstitutions.passage: were rated as high-status whether ... dominant ... or ... submissive

distractors.A: Dominant laughs made low-status individuals seem higher in status, so a dominant laugh does not clearly identify actual status.
distractors.B: Low-status individuals in power produced more dominant, not submissive, laughs.
distractors.C: The passage does not say the two groups’ submissive laughs were surprisingly similar.

questions.prompt: each designed to generate a different kind of ___
questions.evidence: The students then were randomly assigned to watch a video clip eliciting either humour, contentment, or neutral feelings.

synonymSubstitutions.question: generate a different kind of
synonymSubstitutions.passage: eliciting either humour, contentment, or neutral feelings

distractors.A: “a kind of laughter” is not what all three videos generated.
distractors.B: “a kind of relaxing” is ungrammatical and describes only one video.
distractors.C: “a kind of boring” is ungrammatical and is not the three-way category.
distractors.D: Anxiety is not the common category generated by the three videos.
distractors.E: “a kind of stimulating” is ungrammatical and does not name the category.
distractors.G: Enjoyment is only one possible feeling, not the general category.
distractors.H: “a kind of amusing” is ungrammatical; amusing describes the humorous video.

questions.prompt: those who had watched the ___ video
questions.evidence: Students who had watched the Mr. Bean video ended up spending significantly more time working on the task, making twice as many predictions as the other two groups.

synonymSubstitutions.question: persisted with the task for longer
synonymSubstitutions.passage: spending significantly more time working on the task

distractors.A: “laughter video” does not identify any of the three clips.
distractors.B: The relaxing dolphin video was not the group that persisted longest.
distractors.C: “boring video” is not one of the described clips.
distractors.D: “anxiety video” is neither grammatical in context nor described.
distractors.E: The evidence identifies the humorous Mr. Bean clip, not a stimulating clip.
distractors.F: “emotion video” is too general and does not select the successful group.
distractors.G: “enjoyment video” is not the label for the Mr. Bean clip.

questions.prompt: perform a particularly ___ task
questions.evidence: Cheng and Wang then replicated these results in a second study, during which they had participants complete long multiplication questions by hand. Again, participants who watched the humorous video spent significantly more time working on this tedious task and completed more questions correctly than did the students in either of the other groups.

distractors.A: “laughter task” does not describe hand multiplication.
distractors.B: The multiplication task was tedious, not relaxing.
distractors.D: “anxiety task” is not the task description.
distractors.E: The task was not stimulating; humour had an energising effect afterward.
distractors.H: The task itself was not amusing; the video was humorous.

questions.prompt: humour not only reduces ___
questions.evidence: ‘Although humour has been found to help relieve stress and facilitate social relationships, the traditional view of task performance implies that individuals should avoid things such as humour that may distract them from the accomplishment of task goals,’ Cheng and Wang conclude.

distractors.A: Humour may cause laughter; it does not reduce laughter.
distractors.B: “reduces relaxing” is ungrammatical and semantically wrong.
distractors.C: “reduces boring” is ungrammatical; boring is an adjective here.
distractors.E: “reduces stimulating” is ungrammatical and reverses the energising effect.
distractors.F: The findings concern emotional effects, but do not say humour reduces emotion generally.
distractors.G: Humour is enjoyable, so it does not reduce enjoyment.
distractors.H: “reduces amusing” is ungrammatical and contradicts humour.

questions.prompt: it may also have a ___ effect on the body and mind
questions.evidence: ‘We suggest that humour is not only enjoyable but more importantly, energising.’

distractors.A: “a laughter effect” does not paraphrase energising.
distractors.B: A relaxing effect conflicts with the emphasized energising effect.
distractors.C: A boring effect is the opposite of energising.
distractors.D: An anxiety effect is not claimed and conflicts with stress relief.
distractors.F: “an emotion effect” is too vague and unnatural here.
distractors.G: Enjoyment is mentioned, but the summary’s “also” targets the more important energising effect.
distractors.H: “an amusing effect” repeats humour’s enjoyable quality, not its effect on body and mind.

questions.prompt: Participants in the Santa Cruz study were more accurate at identifying the laughs of friends than those of strangers.
questions.evidence: Participants were asked whether they thought the people laughing were friends or strangers. On average, the results were remarkably consistent: worldwide, people’s guesses were correct approximately 60% of the time.

synonymSubstitutions.question: identifying the laughs of friends ... strangers
synonymSubstitutions.passage: whether ... people laughing were friends or strangers

distractors.YES: No separate friend-versus-stranger accuracy rates are stated, so the comparison cannot be confirmed.
distractors.NO: The passage gives no result showing strangers were identified equally or more accurately, so the comparison is not contradicted.

decisionLogic.YES: Not supported: only overall accuracy is given.
decisionLogic.NO: Not supported: no opposite comparison is given.
decisionLogic.NOT_GIVEN: Correct: relative accuracy for friends versus strangers is absent.

questions.prompt: The researchers in the San Diego study were correct in their predictions regarding the behaviour of the high-status individuals.
questions.evidence: Analysis revealed that, as expected, high-status individuals produced more dominant laughs and fewer submissive laughs relative to the low-status individuals.

synonymSubstitutions.question: researchers ... were correct in their predictions
behaviour of the high-status individuals
synonymSubstitutions.passage: high-status individuals produced more dominant laughs and fewer submissive laughs

distractors.NO: “As expected” explicitly says the observed behaviour matched the prediction.
distractors.NOT_GIVEN: The text states both the prediction outcome and the high-status group’s behaviour.

decisionLogic.YES: Correct: observed behaviour occurred as expected.
decisionLogic.NO: Rejected because there is no contradiction.
decisionLogic.NOT_GIVEN: Rejected because the comparison is explicitly reported.

questions.prompt: The participants in the Australian National University study were given a fixed amount of time to complete the task focusing on employee profiles.
questions.evidence: Participants were allowed to quit the task at any point.

synonymSubstitutions.question: given a fixed amount of time
synonymSubstitutions.passage: allowed to quit ... at any point

distractors.YES: A self-chosen stopping point is incompatible with a fixed time allowance.
distractors.NOT_GIVEN: The stopping condition is stated explicitly, so the issue is not missing.

decisionLogic.YES: Rejected: the passage says participants could quit at any point.
decisionLogic.NO: Correct: the statement contradicts the flexible stopping point.

questions.prompt: Cheng and Wang’s conclusions were in line with established notions regarding task performance.
questions.evidence: ‘Although humour has been found to help relieve stress and facilitate social relationships, the traditional view of task performance implies that individuals should avoid things such as humour that may distract them from the accomplishment of task goals,’ Cheng and Wang conclude. ‘We suggest that humour is not only enjoyable but more importantly, energising.’

distractors.YES: Their conclusion challenges the traditional view rather than agreeing with it.
distractors.NOT_GIVEN: Both the traditional view and Cheng and Wang’s contrasting conclusion are explicit.

decisionLogic.YES: Rejected: “energising” opposes the established view that humour distracts from goals.
decisionLogic.NO: Correct: their conclusion is not in line with the traditional notion.
decisionLogic.NOT_GIVEN: Rejected: the relationship is directly inferable from the explicit contrast.
